title: Electrical Work — Fire System Wiring, Panels, Batteries and Mains Supply
verdict:
No. I would not sign this and send a crew out on it.

WHAT IS RIGHT (do not touch it). I pulled the full text of the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) (SL 2026 No. 113, in force 1 Sep 2026) and the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) from legislation.qld.gov.au and checked every citation in the file. All of them are correct, including the wording. s 193 "near ... means within 3m of an exposed energised part"; s 195(1)(a)-(d) the four exceptions, quoted accurately; s 196(2)(a) "each exposed part is treated as energised until it is isolated and found not to be energised"; s 198(2)(a) warning sign having regard to AS 1319 and s 198(2)(b)(i)/(ii) locked open or prevented from accidental closure, with the racking-off and cable-removal examples the SWMS reproduces; s 199(1)(a)-(e) exactly as described; s 200(a)-(d); s 201; s 202; s 203(1)(a)-(c), 203(2) and the s 203(3) testing exception; s 204 (28 days / until complete / 2 years after a serious electrical incident or dangerous electrical event, plus the accessibility and inspection duties); s 211 with no time period of its own, which the SWMS correctly notes; s 229(2)-(4) content and s 229(5) 5-year retention; s 9 standards-in-effect-from-time-to-time; ss 191-192 and "wiring rules means AS/NZS 3000" in schedule 10; and the schedule 10 safety observer definition including the 12-month assessment. On the WHS Regulation side, s 289(2)(e) and s 289(3)(d) are quoted verbatim, s 291(k) is verbatim, and ss 299(2)(d), 300(2), 301, 302 and 303 all say what the document says they say. Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) is SL 2008 No. 160 and is still in force. The JSON shape is exact: all twelve keys, no extras, id unchanged, controls in hierarchy order in every step, residual never above initial. Whoever did the correction pass on the legislation did it properly.

WHY IT STILL FAILS. Two things that can kill or maim are not named anywhere in the file, and one of them is a confirmed offence.

1. Respirable crystalline silica. The cable step has the crew drilling and cutting concrete, masonry, render and tile for penetrations. The word silica does not appear once. There is no P2/RPE in the ppe array, no water suppression, no on-tool extraction, no written assessment. Chapter 8A of the WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) (ss 529A-529L, inserted 2024 SL No. 101, substituted 2024 SL No. 174, amended 2026 SL No. 21) defines "processing" to include "the use of a power tool or mechanical plant to carry out an activity that involves the abrasive polishing, crushing, cutting, drilling, grinding, sanding or trimming of the crystalline silica substance", and a "crystalline silica substance" is any material with at least 1% crystalline silica. Concrete, bricks, mortar and render are expressly named in s 529A as things that are not engineered stone, which means they remain crystalline silica substances. So every masonry penetration on this job is regulated processing. s 529C makes it an offence to carry it out uncontrolled; s 529B requires at least one of isolation, wet suppression, on-tool extraction or LEV, with RPE to AS/NZS 1716 and AS/NZS 1715 for anyone still exposed; s 529CA requires a recorded written assessment before processing starts and expressly forbids relying on PPE or administrative controls in making it. s 529CB(3) lets a SWMS stand in for the silica risk control plan only if the SWMS meets s 529CB(2). This one does not mention the hazard, so it cannot. The document is meticulous about asbestos and blind to the dust the crew will actually make on most jobs.

2. The diesel pumpset. The submain step and the handback step both put a technician in a pump room with a pumpset that will run: "verify auto-start operates". Nothing anywhere covers the drive coupling and shaft guard, the hot exhaust and manifold, or engine exhaust carbon monoxide in an enclosed pump room. The only pump-room control in the entire document is hearing protection. An auto-start on a diesel set with someone at the coupling is an amputation, and CO in a sealed pump room is a fatality with no warning.

Beyond those: the isolation step lists mains, battery, UPS and generator changeover as the sources to kill, and omits rooftop solar PV and battery energy storage, which in 2026 is the second supply most likely to be on a Queensland commercial main switchboard and the one that cannot be killed by opening a switch. The document also defines its own 5x5 bands by consequence and then breaks them: LOW is defined as "minor or insignificant consequence at unlikely or lower" and MEDIUM as "moderate consequence at possible or lower", yet eight steps carrying electrocution, arc blast or an unprotected building are rated MEDIUM or LOW. Consequence does not fall when you apply controls, only likelihood does, so under its own rules every one of those steps floors at HIGH. That is not pedantry: the STOP WORK clause makes the residual rating the trigger for supervisor authorisation, so under-rating the open-FIP step to MEDIUM is what removes the supervisor from live panel work.

Fix those, re-rate, and it becomes a genuinely good document — the legislative work underneath it is the best I have seen on one of these.

WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY. store.standards.org.au returned nothing usable and worksafe.qld.gov.au returned 403 from this session, so I could not confirm current editions of AS 1851, AS 1670.1/.4, AS/NZS 3017, AS IEC 60900, AS 3011.1/.2, AS 2676.1/.2, or the current titles of the Queensland codes of practice. The file cites all of these without years or clause numbers and tells the reader to confirm, which is the safe posture, so I raise no finding — but I am not certifying them either. AS/NZS 3017 is the one I would check hardest before the next revision.

blocking.field: steps[7] ("Cable work — run, terminate and make good to the Wiring Rules") — hazards, controls; also ppe[] and training[]
blocking.problem: Respirable crystalline silica is not named anywhere in the document. The step has the crew drilling and cutting concrete, masonry, render and tile for cable penetrations. There is no RPE in the ppe array, no wet suppression or on-tool extraction control, and no written assessment. Verified against legislation.qld.gov.au: WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) ch 8A (ss 529A-529L, ins 2024 SL No. 101, sub 2024 SL No. 174, amd 2026 SL No. 21). s 529A defines "processing" to include "the use of a power tool or mechanical plant to carry out an activity that involves the abrasive polishing, crushing, cutting, drilling, grinding, sanding or trimming of the crystalline silica substance", and "crystalline silica substance" as "material that contains at least 1% crystalline silica"; concrete, bricks, mortar, render and tiles are expressly excluded from "engineered stone" but remain crystalline silica substances. s 529C: a PCBU "must not carry out, or direct or allow a worker to carry out, the processing of a crystalline silica substance unless the processing is controlled" (60 penalty units). s 529B requires at least one of isolation from dust, wet suppression, on-tool extraction or LEV, plus RPE complying with AS/NZS 1716 and AS/NZS 1715 for anyone still at risk. s 529CA(1) and (4) require a written assessment before processing starts; s 529CA(3) forbids having regard to PPE or administrative controls in making it. s 529CB(3) allows the SWMS to substitute for a silica risk control plan only if it satisfies s 529CB(2) — this one cannot, because it does not mention the hazard.
blocking.fix: Add silica to steps[7].hazards ("drilling, cutting or chasing concrete, masonry, render or tile — respirable crystalline silica, silicosis"). Add controls in order: eliminate — use an existing penetration or a core already there, or reroute to a clear substrate; substitute — hand-punch or a non-powered method where the penetration allows; engineering — on-tool dust extraction with an H-class vacuum, or wet suppression, on every powered drill, saw or chase into masonry; administrative — a written assessment recorded on the job card before the first hole, made without regard to PPE or administrative controls, deciding whether the processing is high risk; and confirm this SWMS states the silica control measures and how they are implemented, monitored and reviewed so it can stand as the silica risk control plan. Add to ppe[]: a P2 (or better) respirator complying with AS/NZS 1716, selected, fitted and maintained to AS/NZS 1715, fit-tested and clean-shaven. Add to training[]: silica awareness and RPE fit-testing. Add a siteSpecificPrompt asking what the wall, floor and backing board are made of and what dust control is on the vehicle. Cite the obligation in words and name the instrument as "Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), chapter 8A (crystalline silica)".

blocking.field: steps[8] ("Work on the submain feeding the fire pump") and steps[10] ("Re-energise, restore the fire system and the pumpset, and hand it back") — hazards and controls
blocking.problem: The document puts a technician in a pump room with a pumpset that will start — steps[10] requires "verify auto-start operates" — and names none of the mechanical or atmospheric hazards of a diesel pumpset. Nothing anywhere covers the drive coupling and shaft guard (entanglement, amputation on auto-start), the hot exhaust manifold, turbo and engine block (contact burns), or engine exhaust carbon monoxide accumulating in an enclosed pump room during a test run. The only pump-room control in the whole file is "Hearing protection in the pump room whenever the pumpset may run". AS 2941 pumpsets on Queensland sites are frequently diesel, and the step already contemplates the set starting unexpectedly ("The pumpset starting on you mid-job from the pressure line, the jockey pump, or an auto-start signal") without carrying that through to what the running machine does to a person standing next to it.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[8].hazards and steps[10].hazards: rotating shaft, coupling and drive guard on a set that can auto-start; hot exhaust, manifold and engine surfaces; carbon monoxide from a diesel engine run in an enclosed pump room; the pumpset's own diesel starting batteries. Add controls: isolate — the engine start circuit and both starting batteries isolated and locked, not only the electrical submain, before anyone is within reach of the coupling; engineering — coupling and drive guards confirmed in place and secured before any run, and pump room ventilation and exhaust flue proved clear and open before a diesel run; administrative — nobody inside the coupling guard line or between the engine and the wall during a run; keep clear of exhaust and manifold for the cool-down period; if the room has no proved ventilation path, the run is done with the door open and nobody in the room, or the room is gas-tested. Add a siteSpecificPrompt: "Is the pumpset electric or diesel? Where are its starting batteries and its start circuit isolator, is the coupling guard intact, and does the room have a proved exhaust flue and ventilation for a diesel run?"

blocking.field: steps[2] ("Find the supply, isolate it, lock it, tag it, keep the key on you") — controls, third entry; also steps[3].hazards and siteSpecificPrompts
blocking.problem: The "kill every source" control lists "mains breaker, the panel battery link or fuse, any UPS, and the generator changeover feeding the same board" and omits rooftop solar PV and battery energy storage. The siteSpecificPrompt asking about a second supply lists "UPS, generator changeover, a networked sub-panel, or a shared neutral" and again omits PV. On a 2026 Queensland commercial building, PV on the main switchboard is the norm, and it is the one source that behaves differently from every other item on that list: the array DC is live in daylight regardless of any switch position, and an inverter can hold a voltage on the AC side for seconds after the AC breaker opens. A technician who works the list as written can lock every device named on it and still be in front of a live board.
blocking.fix: Add solar PV inverter supply and any battery energy storage system to the steps[2] "kill every source" control, with the specific instruction that the PV AC breaker is opened, the DC isolator at the array and at the inverter is opened and locked, and the inverter is given its rated discharge time before anything is touched — and that the array DC conductors remain live in daylight and are never assumed dead. Add "backfeed from a solar PV inverter or a battery energy storage system on the same board" to steps[3].hazards. Amend the siteSpecificPrompt to read "...UPS, generator changeover, solar PV inverter, battery energy storage, a networked sub-panel, or a shared neutral with another circuit?"

blocking.field: whenRequired (the "HOW RISK IS RATED IN THIS DOCUMENT" matrix) against residualRisk on steps[0], [1], [2], [3], [4], [6], [7], [8], [9] and [10]
blocking.problem: The document defines its own bands by consequence and likelihood — "LOW — minor or insignificant consequence at unlikely or lower", "MEDIUM — moderate consequence at possible or lower, or minor at likely or higher", "HIGH — catastrophic or major consequence at unlikely likelihood, or moderate at likely or higher" — and then rates ten of eleven steps below what those bands allow. Applying controls lowers likelihood; it does not lower consequence. Every one of these steps carries a hazard the document itself classes as Catastrophic (electrocution, arc blast, an unprotected building that burns), so under its own definitions each floors at HIGH, and the matrix leaves no band at all for a catastrophic consequence at "rare". This is not a paperwork point: the STOP WORK clause makes the residual rating the trigger — "A residual risk of HIGH is not a licence to proceed — it means the work does not go ahead on the technician's own authority." Rating steps[4] ("Open the fire indicator panel and work inside it", initial extreme) at MEDIUM is what takes the supervisor out of live panel work. steps[9] and steps[10] are rated LOW while carrying "Energising onto a fault — arc flash at the board", "Missing or high-resistance earth leaving the panel enclosure live under fault", "Closing the breaker while someone still has hands in the panel" and "Client believing the system is protecting them when it is not".
blocking.fix: Pick one and make it consistent. Either (a) rewrite the band definitions so they are genuinely two-dimensional and state a floor — e.g. that a step retaining a credible fatality mechanism cannot be rated below HIGH regardless of likelihood, which is what the document's STOP WORK clause already assumes; or (b) leave the bands alone and re-rate: steps[2], [3], [4], [6] and [8] to HIGH, steps[1], [7], [9] and [10] to MEDIUM, and steps[0] to MEDIUM. Option (b) is the honest one and matches how steps[5] was rated. Then check the STOP WORK clause still reads correctly against the new ratings, since it will now gate most of the job through the supervisor — which is the correct outcome for energised fire panel and switchboard work.

blocking.field: steps[8] ("Work on the submain feeding the fire pump") — residualRisk and controls
blocking.problem: Two problems in the same step. First, residualRisk is "medium" on a step whose own hazard list concedes "The busbar and the supply side of the fire pump breaker stay live and cannot be isolated at the board — the breaker can be dead on the load side while its own terminals are live behind it", at the highest fault-energy board on the site. steps[5] honestly holds its residual at HIGH for lower-energy energised testing at a FIP. The same document cannot rate un-isolatable live busbars at a main switchboard a band lower than probing a fire panel. Second, the controls array contains no safety observer control at all — the observer appears only in the "responsible" string and in a control that says to brief "the observer" by pointing, with no requirement that one be present or that they meet the definition. Verified: Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 203(1)(c) requires the work to be "observed by a safety observer" subject only to the s 203(3) testing exception, which does not cover working at an open switchboard with exposed live busbars.
blocking.fix: Raise steps[8].residualRisk to "high" and add a STOP WORK control mirroring the one in steps[5], so the step goes back to the supervisor rather than proceeding on the technician's authority. Add an explicit administrative control requiring a safety observer meeting the schedule 10 definition, present and doing nothing else, whenever the busbar chamber or the supply side of the breaker is exposed, citing Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 203(1)(c). Also add, to the isolate controls, a stored-energy check for any soft starter or variable speed drive in the pump controller — proved dead on the DC bus after the manufacturer's discharge time, not just on the incoming supply.

blocking.field: steps[7].controls[0] and steps[7].controls[3] (level fields); steps[1].controls[0] (level field)
blocking.problem: Three controls sit at levels they do not belong to. steps[7].controls[0] is labelled "eliminate" but reads "Consult the site asbestos register and the asbestos management plan BEFORE any drilling, cutting, sanding or fixing" — reading a document is an administrative control; it eliminates nothing, and it occupies the top-of-hierarchy slot in the one step that most needs a real elimination control. steps[7].controls[3] is labelled "engineering" but reads "Where a route cannot avoid material that is or is presumed to be asbestos, reroute — surface mount, use an existing penetration, or come in from a clear substrate" — rerouting so the hazard is never created is elimination, and it has been demoted two levels. So the step's only genuine elimination control is buried in the middle and the top slot is paperwork. steps[1].controls[0] is labelled "isolate" but reads "Ring the monitoring provider and isolate the ASE for this job" — that is the fire system's own "isolate" function, not isolation in the hierarchy of control, and it is the act that creates the step's hazard (a building with no automatic brigade call), not a control on it. Strip the mislabel and steps[1] is administrative-only.
blocking.fix: Re-level steps[7].controls[0] to "administrative" and steps[7].controls[3] to "eliminate", and reorder the array so the reroute control leads the step. Re-level steps[1].controls[0] to "administrative". Then re-check steps[1]: with no control above administrative it needs either a genuine higher-order control (schedule the impairment so the building is occupied and staffed, or stage the work so only one zone is out at a time) or an honest residual rating. Nothing else in the file needs re-levelling — the remaining controls sit correctly.

blocking.field: steps[] as a whole — no step covers access; training[] mentions height access but no control implements it
blocking.problem: Falls below 2 m have no control anywhere in the document. The activity line includes "running and terminating cable", which on a real job means a stepladder or a platform at a riser, a cable tray, an EWIS speaker or a detector base. whenRequired correctly pushes falls of more than 2 m out to a separate SWMS under WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 291(a) (verified verbatim), and training[] mentions a working-at-heights and EWP ticket above 2 m — so the document knows ladders will be used, and then controls nothing below the HRCW threshold, which is exactly where no second SWMS will ever be triggered. Nothing selects or inspects a ladder, requires it to be footed or tied, or — most importantly — forbids energised work or live proving from a ladder. Working live off a ladder is a standard electrical fatality mechanism: the shock does not have to be the thing that kills you.
blocking.fix: Add access controls to steps[4], [5] and [7]: engineering — a platform ladder or podium step with a handrail in preference to a leaning or step ladder wherever the work needs two hands or takes more than a moment; administrative — ladder inspected and rated for the load, set on a firm level base, footed or secured, three points of contact, nothing carried up by hand; and an explicit prohibition — no energised work, no proving dead and no work inside an open panel is performed from a ladder or any unstable platform; if the panel cannot be reached from the floor or a platform with a handrail, the work is done dead or the access is changed. Add a siteSpecificPrompt asking how each panel, rack and cable run will be reached and what access equipment is on the vehicle.

blocking.field: steps[6] ("Replace the battery bank") — controls[0] against controls[1]
blocking.problem: The step contradicts itself. controls[0] (eliminate) says that if the bank is vented (flooded) cells or sits in a dedicated battery room, "STOP ... Do not open it, do not disconnect it, do not switch anything in that room", and the permits array and siteSpecificPrompts both say vented cells are out of scope of this SWMS. controls[1] (substitute) then says "Where the panel manufacturer and AS 1670.1 permit it, fit sealed VRLA cells in place of vented cells" — which is work on a vented bank, under this SWMS, that controls[0] has just prohibited. A crew reading down the list in order gets a stop and then an instruction to proceed on the same cells.
blocking.fix: Either delete controls[1] from steps[6], or rewrite it so it is plainly a design recommendation made from the office and not an on-the-tools instruction — e.g. "Where a site has vented cells, raise a recommendation with the office to convert the bank to sealed VRLA where the panel manufacturer and AS 1670.1 permit. That conversion is planned and quoted separately and is carried out under the flammable atmosphere SWMS, not this one." Keep it at "substitute" if reworded; the substitution is real, it just is not this crew's job today.

blocking.problem: The control says "note that s 199(2)(a) relaxes only the 'clear of obstructions' precondition for that work, not the risk assessment, the SWMS, the isolation point requirement or the authorisation". That is correct as far as it goes and I confirmed it against the text, but it omits the second limb. Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 199(2)(a) has two cumulative conditions: "(i) the work is to be performed on the supply side of the main switch on the main switchboard for the equipment; and (ii) the point at which the equipment can be disconnected from its electricity supply is not reasonably accessible from the work location". As written the SWMS implies that being on the supply side of the main switch is enough on its own.
blocking.fix: Amend the control to state both limbs: the relief from the clear-of-obstructions precondition applies only where the work is on the supply side of the main switch AND the disconnection point is not reasonably accessible from the work location. If the disconnection point is reasonably accessible, s 199(1)(c) applies in full.

blocking.field: steps[10] ("Re-energise, restore the fire system and the pumpset, and hand it back") — controls; and references[] (Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 entry)
blocking.problem: No control anywhere covers the critical defect notice. Verified: Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) is SL 2008 No. 160 and remains in force. s 53 places the duty on the person who carried out the maintenance — the Safe QLD technician, not the occupier — to give the occupier a notice in the approved form within 24 hours of carrying out the maintenance, where they become aware or ought reasonably to be aware of a critical defect (30 penalty units). s 49 defines a critical defect as one likely to render the installation inoperable and reasonably likely to have a significant adverse impact on occupant safety, with "a defect making a fire detection and alarm system inoperable" and "a defect in a pump making the fire hydrants for a building inoperable" given as the examples — precisely the outcomes this SWMS's steps can leave behind. The document handles the occupier's maintenance duty and the AS 1851 log book thoroughly and never mentions this duty, which falls on the crew.
blocking.fix: Add an administrative control to steps[10]: "If you leave site with a defect that renders the detection and alarm system, or the pump feeding the hydrants, inoperable, give the occupier a critical defect notice in the approved form within 24 hours — that duty is on the person who carried out the maintenance, not on the occupier (Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld), s 53). Tell the office the same day so the notice actually goes out." Extend the references[] entry to read "Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) — occupier's duty to maintain prescribed fire safety installations and to give the occupier statement, and the maintainer's duty under s 53 to give a critical defect notice within 24 hours".

blocking.field: ppe[] and steps[4], [5], [8] — no heat control
blocking.problem: Heat is not mentioned anywhere. The document requires arc-rated long sleeves and trousers, an arc-rated balaclava, a face shield, insulating gloves with leather overgloves and a hard hat, and puts the crew in Queensland plant rooms, roof-level risers and switchrooms — routinely well over 40 degrees in summer with no ventilation — and frequently on an after-hours shift with a two-person crew and nobody else in the building. Heat illness under full arc-rated layering is a real collapse mechanism, and a technician who goes down from heat in front of an open live panel is in the same position as one who has taken a shock.
blocking.fix: Add a heat hazard to steps[4], [5] and [8] and an administrative control: check plant room temperature and ventilation before starting; water and a shaded or air-conditioned break area identified before the first cover comes off; scheduled rest breaks out of the arc-rated layers when working in an unventilated plant room; the observer watches the worker for heat symptoms as well as for electrical risk; and the work stops if either worker shows them. Add a siteSpecificPrompt: "How hot is the plant room or riser, is there any ventilation or cooling, and where is the nearest shaded or air-conditioned break space?" Add heat illness recognition and first aid to the emergency string.

blocking.problem: Labelled "isolate" but reads "The door interlock, the key switch and the panel ON/OFF are not isolations. The only isolation is the breaker at the board, locked and tagged as set out in the isolation step." That is a rule about what does not count as isolation — a correct and valuable one — but it is an administrative statement, not an isolating control. It occupies an isolate slot ahead of the two controls in the same step that do genuinely isolate (shrouding and barriering, and locking every feeding panel on a networked system).
blocking.fix: Re-level steps[4].controls[1] to "administrative" and move it below the genuine isolate controls, or fold its wording into the shrouding control so the step keeps the warning without misrepresenting its level.
